clue.text: Told son to take plane

parts.note: told, as in said or uttered, means spoke
S is the standard abbreviation for son in genealogies
to take, as in to have a drink or a meal, is to have

explanation.surface: Someone instructed their son to catch a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' looks like an aircraft but it is the woodworking tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A spokeshave is a small two-handled carpenter's tool, a kind of plane for shaping curved wood such as wheel spokes.

clue.text: Thirty days for this group of Irishmen

explanation.surface: A month during which this Irish band gathers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sept. is short for September, a month of thirty days, and a sept is an Irish clan or family division.

clue.text: Spoken, or could be sung, after church

indicators.note: after means what is left once the church has been taken away from the front

parts.note: choral describes music written for a choir to sing

explanation.surface: Words may be spoken or sung after a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove CH from CHORAL and what remains, coming after it, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral means by word of mouth, as in an oral exam.

clue.text: Pure mince is a recipe for the enjoyment of good food

indicators.note: a recipe is a set of instructions for combining ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Fine mince meat is a recipe for gourmet pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' is the anagram signal, rearranging PURE MINCE IS A.
explanation.definitionFit: Epicureanism, after the philosopher Epicurus, is now the devotion to fine eating and drinking.

clue.text: Damage round top of sycamore trees

definitions.note: the plural trees defines a single word naming a group of them, a wood

indicators.note: round says the first piece goes around the letter that follows

parts.note: to damage is to hurt

indicators.note: top of in a down clue means the first letter of the word sycamore

explanation.surface: Harming the crown of a sycamore damages the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurst is an old word for a wooded hill or grove, a small stand of woodland.

clue.text: Railway servant carrying gar- ment for parishioner

indicators.note: in a down clue the railway servant carries the garment on top, so the garment comes first

parts.note: a vest is an undergarment
a man is a manservant

explanation.surface: A railway worker is carrying clothing for a member of the parish.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'carrying' puts the garment above, so before, the railway servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestryman is a parishioner elected to the vestry, the body that runs a parish's affairs.

clue.text: Stonework by a lake

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A piece of masonry stands beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word 'Stonework' has to be split into 'Stone' and 'work': the definition and a piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Opal is a precious gemstone, prized for its shifting play of colours.

clue.text: Going up and down like a gig perhaps

definitions.text: Going up and down like a gig perhaps

parts.words: Going up and down like a gig perhaps
parts.note: a word such as gig reads the same in a down entry from top to bottom and bottom to top

explanation.surface: Moving up and down, as one might at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gig' looks like a pop concert, but it is an example of a word that reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: A word that reads identically forwards and backwards, like gig or level, has this property.

clue.text: A persistent flasher at the seaside

definitions.text: A persistent flasher at the seaside

parts.words: A persistent flasher at the seaside
parts.note: a coastal tower whose beam flashes again and again through the night

explanation.surface: A man exposing himself repeatedly on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flasher' suggests an indecent exposer but means something whose light flashes.
explanation.definitionFit: This coastal tower shines a regularly flashing beam to warn ships.

clue.text: Similar page almost enough to produce evidence of this

definitions.text: Similar page almost enough to produce evidence of this

indicators.note: to produce here is to make something new out of these letters, so they are rearranged
almost the whole word page means it loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A page close enough to another one counts as proof of copying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims PAGE to PAG; 'produce' then rearranges SIMILAR plus PAG. The whole clue also defines: a near-identical page is the evidence of copying.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying another writer's work and passing it off as one's own is shown by pages that closely match the original.

clue.text: Pellet for garden pest

explanation.surface: A pellet meant to deal with a garden pest.
explanation.definitionFit: A lead bullet or airgun pellet is called a slug, and so is the shell-less mollusc that eats lettuces.

clue.text: Tense athlete — Cantab?

parts.note: a tense person is electric with nerves, and a Cambridge sportsman is a Blue, together naming a vivid colour

explanation.surface: A nervous Cambridge sportsman is about to compete.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is someone who has represented Oxford or Cambridge at a sport; Cantab means of Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: This vivid, bright steely shade of blue takes its name from the colour of an electric spark.

clue.text: The fixer is winged

parts.note: a fastener whose head has two flat wings for turning by hand, suggesting an insect

explanation.surface: Someone who fixes things has suddenly sprouted wings.
explanation.definitionFit: This threaded fastener has two flat lugs, like an insect's wings, so it can be tightened by finger and thumb.

clue.text: He takes the top stream, possibly

definitions.text: He takes the top stream, possibly

parts.words: He takes the top stream, possibly
parts.note: a school's chief teacher might teach the highest set, which in British schools is called a stream

explanation.surface: Someone who goes to the source of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a stream is a class grouped by ability; it also suggests a river whose head is its source.
explanation.definitionFit: The man in charge of a school, its principal, might teach the brightest class.

clue.text: Sound recorder for a specialist

parts.note: an instrument an ear doctor uses to measure a patient's hearing

explanation.surface: A tape machine bought for an expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound recorder' suggests a tape machine; it is a device that measures hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: An audiometer is a device used by hearing specialists to test how well someone hears tones.

clue.text: Immense copper involved in search of the whole church

indicators.note: letters that are involved get tangled up, so the word Immense and the copper are mixed together

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A huge policeman is taking part in a nationwide search of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer but gives the chemical symbol CU, which 'involved in' mixes with IMMENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The ecumenical movement seeks unity among all Christian denominations, a quest to bring together the universal church.

clue.text: Paddy and animal in a ludicrous argument

parts.note: Paddy, from Patrick, is an old slang name for an Irishman, so stands for Irish
a bull is a male bovine animal

explanation.surface: An Irishman and a beast caught up in a silly quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish bull is a self-contradictory statement, like 'If you don't get this, write and tell me'.

clue.text: The dog I love is a rarity

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: My beloved dog is an unusual creature.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis 'love' means a score of zero, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: A curio is an unusual or rare object, the kind of collectable oddity people seek out.

clue.text: Heard great one condescend

indicators.note: heard tells us the word is spoken, so we want something that sounds like the next piece

parts.note: a Great Dane is a breed of dog, so a great one is a Dane

explanation.surface: Someone overheard a grand person stooping to their level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great one' suggests an important person, but read it as a Great Dane, the large dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: To deign is to do something one considers beneath one's dignity, which is to condescend.

clue.text: Within limits, signora must be a fool

indicators.note: the letters lie inside the boundaries of the words, with only the outer letter at each end dropped

explanation.surface: An Italian lady, within reason, must be a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within limits' sounds like moderation; here it means drop the first and last letters of SIGNORAMUST.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant, foolish person, a dunce.

clue.text: Disturbances of the environment by sulphur

parts.note: atmospheric means relating to the air or surroundings, the environment
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: Sulphur emissions are disturbing the environment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests pollution, but 'Disturbances' is the definition and 'by' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Atmospherics is radio interference caused by electrical activity in the air, crackling disturbances on the signal.

clue.text: Have a quick look and see Ro- man King in the lead

indicators.note: in the lead puts the king at the front of the word that follows

parts.note: R, from the Latin rex, is the abbreviation for king
ecce is Latin for see or behold

explanation.surface: Take a quick look and see the Roman king leading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see Roman' means the Latin word for 'see'; R is Latin rex, king.
explanation.definitionFit: A recce, short for reconnaissance, is a quick survey of an area before acting.

clue.text: No revolutionary church formerly

indicators.note: a revolutionary word turns right round, so the letters of No are read backwards

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: No church was ever revolutionary in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reverses NO to ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means at one time in the past, as in 'once upon a time'.

clue.text: River takes two lives

indicators.note: two means the word is taken twice over, one copy after the other

parts.note: lives means exists, which is to say is

explanation.surface: A river claims two people's lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isis is the name for the Thames as it flows through Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isis is the stretch of the River Thames at Oxford.

clue.text: Carry little one easily at first

parts.note: a tot is a small child, a little one

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of the word easily is used

explanation.surface: Someone carries a small child without effort, to begin with.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to carry or lug something about, as in toting a bag.

clue.text: The lusciousness, say, of prickly pears

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken aloud, so we want a word with the same sound

parts.note: succulence is juiciness, lusciousness

explanation.surface: Prickly pears are prized for their juicy flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like 'for example' but here signals a soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: Prickly pears are cacti, which store water in fleshy stems and so are classed as succulent plants.

clue.text: Two lots of soldiers not widely known

parts.note: the Royal Artillery is the RA and the Royal Engineers the RE, two British army corps
the Royal Artillery is the RA and the Royal Engineers the RE, two British army corps

explanation.surface: Two military units whose names few people know.
explanation.walkthrough: RA and RE are crossword-standard abbreviations for two British army corps, the Royal Artillery and the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is uncommon, seldom found or heard of.

clue.text: Futile, being unarmed

explanation.surface: A pointless effort by someone without weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeveless once meant futile, as in a sleeveless errand, and a garment without arms is literally sleeveless.
